'''Charles Panati''' (born March 13, 1943) is a former college professor, industrial physicist, author and science editor of ''[[Newsweek]]''.<ref>{{cite news |first= Eric |last= Kinkopf |date= August 28, 1987 |url= https://www.proquest.com/docview/291052009 |title= The extraordinary electric iron, and other tidbits |newspaper= [[Chicago Tribune]] |page= 3 |id= {{ProQuest|291052009}} |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Biography ==

Panati was born in [[Baltimore]], Maryland, and raised in [[Atlantic City, New Jersey]]. After graduating from [[Villanova University]] (1961–65) with a B.S. in physics, Panati obtained a master's degree in Radiation Health Physics (1966) from [[Columbia University]] and worked in cancer research at the [[Columbia Presbyterian Hospital]]. Panati is openly gay.<ref>{{cite news |last= Panati |first= Charles |date= June 23, 1998 |title= Faithful in our fashion: In nature, as mirrored in gay male life, monogamy does not necessarily imply fidelity |magazine= [[The Advocate (LGBT magazine)|The Advocate]] |volume= 762 |page= 11 |id= {{ProQuest|215760591}} }}</ref>

== Parapsychology ==

After joining ''[[Newsweek]]'' in 1971, Panati became interested in [[parapsychology]] and published his first book, ''Supersenses: Our Potential For Parasensory Experience'' (1974), which described parapsychological research into [[extrasensory perception]]. The book was described in a review as a respectable survey of psi phenomena but "the skeptic will remain unconvinced... because the subject is not amenable to rational, empirical scrutiny."<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/charles-panati-2/supersenses-our-potential-for-parasensory-exper/ |title= Supersenses: Our Potential for Parasensory Experience |magazine= [[Kirkus Reviews]] |accessdate= April 16, 2014 |type= book review}}</ref> Panati later met the Israeli psychic [[Uri Geller]], who suggested Panati collect and publish 22 research papers by scientists around the world who had investigated the [[Spoon bending|spoon-bender]]'s alleged abilities. ''The Geller Papers'' (1976), edited by Panati, caused controversy when it was published. Several prominent magicians came forward to demonstrate that Geller's so-called psychic talents could be easily duplicated by stage magicians. Science writer [[Martin Gardner]] wrote that Panati had been fooled by Geller's trickery and ''The Geller Papers'' were an "embarrassing anthology".<ref>{{cite book |last= Gardner |first= Martin |authorlink= Martin Gardner |year= 2003 |title= Are Universes Thicker Than Blackberries? |publisher= [[W. W. Norton & Company|W.W. Norton & Co.]] |pages= [https://archive.org/details/areuniversesthic0000gard/page/244 244–5] |isbn= 9780393057423 |url= https://archive.org/details/areuniversesthic0000gard/page/244 }}</ref> In ''Death Encounters'' (1979), Panati investigated the phenomenon of [[clinical death]], in which subjects report being drawn toward a white light while wrestling with the will to live. ''[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]'' writer Wendy Thomson Warner wrote that, "His views on parapsychology have, rightly or wrongly, been the target of widespread skepticism in the scientific community."<ref name=Pittsburg>{{cite news |last= Warner |first= Wendy Thomson |title= Provocative look at hazards of radiation |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19810521&id=T4NIAAAAIBAJ&sjid=020DAAAAIBAJ&pg=2055,3845560 |accessdate= April 16, 2014 |newspaper= [[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |date= May 21, 1981 |via= [[Google News]]}}</ref>

== ''Origins'' book series ==

Panati has written a series of books about the origins of ordinary, everyday things, beginning in 1984 with ''The Browser’s Book of Beginnings.'' He wrote a second book, ''Extraordinary Origins of Everyday Things'' in 1987 that was praised as "excellent bathroom reading".<ref name=NAS>{{cite news |title= Bored with the baby boomers |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1917&dat=19870824&id=Cg0hAAAAIBAJ&sjid=b3IFAAAAIBAJ&pg=2823,5648209 |accessdate=April 16, 2014 |newspaper= [[The Daily Gazette|Schenectady Gazette]] |date= August 24, 1987 |last= Shearer |first= Cody |page= 22 |via= [[Google News]]}}</ref> Subsequent books in the series were ''Panati’s Parade of Fads, Follies and Manias: The Origins of Our Most Cherished Obsessions'' in 1991, ''Sacred Origins of Profound Things: The Stories Behind the Rites and Rituals of the World’s Religions'' in 1996, ''Sexy Origins of Intimate Things'' in 1998, and ''Words To Live By: Origins of Common Wisdom Expressions'' in 1999.

His book ''Extraordinary Origins of Everyday Things'' has been described as a "handy reference".<ref>{{cite news |last= Martin |first= Susan |date= December 23, 1992 |title= Why all these traditions? Exploring the origins of some holiday customs |newspaper= [[The Buffalo News]] |access-date= April 16, 2014 |url= http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-22446178.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140611124123/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P2-22446178.html |url-status= usurped |archive-date= June 11, 2014 |url-access= subscription |location= Buffalo, NY |via= [[HighBeam Research]]}}</ref> Panati's ''Sacred Origins of Profound Things'' received a positive review and was described as "an informative and entertaining book on the origins of religious ideas, sacred items, worship practices, holy symbols, and holidays."<ref>{{cite journal |last= Masuchika |first= Glenn |date=December 1996 |title= Sacred Origins of Profound Things: The Stories Behind the Rites and Rituals of the World's Religions |journal= [[Library Journal]] |volume= 121 |issue= 20 |page= 100 |id= {{ProQuest|196681718}} }}</ref>

==''The Silent Intruder: Surviving the Radiation Age''==

In 1981, Panati and his brother, Michael Hudson, wrote ''The Silent Intruder: Surviving the Radiation Age'', a book that seeks to examine the interaction of radiation and human tissue.<ref name=Pittsburg />

== Media ==

Panati has appeared as a guest on ''[[The Oprah Winfrey Show|Oprah]]'', Regis and ''[[Late Show with David Letterman|Letterman]]''.
